card.title: Short Story 3 — God Sees the Truth but Waits (Leo Tolstoy)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The story at a glance "God Sees the Truth, but Waits" by Leo Tolstoy is a parable of injustice and forgiveness: Ivan Dmitrich Aksionov, a prosperous merchant with a slight weakness for drink, is falsely accused of murdering a fellow merchant, flogged, and sent to Siberia for twenty-six years. In the prison he becomes a holy man — and then the real murderer, Makar Semyonich, is placed in the same cell.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Theme: divine justice vs human justice — Aksionov suffers for a crime he did not commit.
The title's meaning: God sees the truth but waits 26 years; forgiveness ends the story.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: Character change question: track Aksyonov from carefree merchant to spiritual, resigned prisoner — pick two contrasting moments (early suspicion of wife; final forgiveness).  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **Ivan Dmitrich Aksionov** is the story's long arc: merchant → accused → convict → saint. The sketch the exam wants has its hinges: the drink that makes the accusation plausible, the cry of "It is not my sin!" that shows his innocence is not serenity but protest, the years that turn protest into peace, and the final forgiveness that completes him.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **Injustice and endurance** — the state can take everything except the soul's response; Aksionov's twenty-six years are the theme in duration. **Forgiveness** — the story's summit: forgiveness given freely, without apology received first, and its double rescue.…  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"Why was Aksionov sentenced though innocent?" (4 marks)** — the planted knife, the blood-stained coat, the lack of proof; state the irony of fate by name. **"How did Aksionov change in Siberia?"** — the arc from protest to peace; the boots, the scripture, the nickname Grandfather.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. What is the significance of the title? (2 marks) — God knows the truth but his justice comes in his own time; Aksyonov's 26-year wait shows this.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **‘God Sees the Truth, but Waits’ — moral architecture (classified)** | Theme | Development | Evidence | |---|---|---| | Injustice | Wrongful conviction of Aksionov | Sear-skin, bloody knife | | Forgiveness | He pardons Makar Semyonich | Refuses to inform | | Truth delayed | Real killer confesses too late | Order already signed | | Divine justice | Earthly courts err; God waits | Title itself |  ·  **Aksionov’s transformation** | Stage | State | Sign | |---|---|---| | Merchant | Carefree, respected | Fair, sanguine | | Prisoner | Despair, prayer | Loses wife’s trust | | Elder | God-fearing, gentle | ‘Grandfather’ to inmates | | Forgiver | Peace beyond verdict | Lets hatred die |

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns The tragedy is set up in two strokes: Aksionov is young, merry, and fond of drink, and a rival merchant stays the night with him. On the road, a soldier asks whose blood is on his coat — the fellow merchant has been found murdered, and a blood-stained knife is discovered in Aksionov's bag.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Irony of fate** — the master device: the innocent man is convicted on evidence the guilty man planted, and lives the sentence; the blood-stained knife is the story's whole injustice in one image. - **Dramatic irony** — the reader watches the wife doubt him, the courts err, and the years pass, knowing what none of them know.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Theme in one line: divine justice and forgiveness outweigh human law — Ivan's pardon of Makar is the proof event; quote it.  ·  Trick 2: Irony is the device to name: the title promises God sees the truth but WAITS — 26 years of suffering before truth emerges; explain the double irony (Makar confesses, Aksyonov dies before release).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. How does Aksyonov change in Siberia? (2 marks) — from a worldly, quick-tempered merchant to a saintly, forgiving man.
